title: "Exercise 3.1b — One workflow, two models"

*HDS MSc · Module 3 · the R version of this exercise; the web page is at <https://inflamuob.github.io/HDS_M3/day3/day3-01b-one-workflow.html>.*

*Open it in Positron or RStudio and run it a chunk at a time. Keep it in the folder that holds your `data` folder. Cells with `______` are blanks for you to fill in.*

In R, you can fit a linear regression directly with `lm()`. In this practical
you will use `lm()` as the engine inside the familiar tidymodels steps:
**specify** a model, **fit** it on training patients, and call **`predict()`**
for held-out patients. In Python the same three steps are
`LinearRegression()`, `.fit()` and `.predict()` from scikit-learn.

- **Part 1.** Predict blood glucose from age. Calculate the prediction for a
  45-year-old by hand from the fitted equation, check it with `predict()`, and
  see the point on the fitted line. Compare predictions with the measured
  glucose of the test patients, then refit with different training patients
  to see how the line and the predictions change.
- **Part 2.** Add BMI, repeat the hand calculation, and find the prediction on
  the fitted plane in a 3D plot you can turn.
- **Part 3.** Keep the same steps, training patients and predictors, and fit a
  decision tree instead. Follow the same patient through the splits, read the
  prediction from the leaf, check it with `predict()`, and compare the tree's
  stepped surface with the regression plane.

> **The plots are for looking at**
>
> The code for every plot is included, so that you can run it and see the figure. You are not expected to write it yourself.

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot", "plotly"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)

theme_set(theme_bw())
```

`data/glucose_bmi_study.csv` holds 77 patients with three columns: age in
years, BMI in kg/m² and blood glucose in mg/dL. If you do not have it yet, [**download `glucose_bmi_study.csv`**](data/glucose_bmi_study.csv)
into your `data` folder.

```{r}
glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_bmi_study.csv")

summary(glu)
```

Split the 77 patients into training and test patients, as on Day 1.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8)

train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

cat(nrow(train), "training patients,", nrow(test), "test patients\n")
```

### Part 1 — Predict glucose from age

The same three steps as on Day 1: specify the model, fit it on the training
patients, predict.

```{r}
# 1. Specify: linear regression, computed by lm()
lm_model <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

# 2. Fit on the training patients
line_fit <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = train)

# the learned parameters: intercept first, then the slope
b <- line_fit$fit$coefficients
b
```

The fitted equation is

$$\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age}$$

#### Task 1a — A 45-year-old, by hand

Read the two parameters printed above, round them to two decimals, and
calculate the predicted glucose for a 45-year-old.

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_45 <- ______ + ______ * 45
predicted_45
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> The first number is the intercept, $\hat\beta_0$. The second is the slope,
> $\hat\beta_1$, which multiplies the age.

Now check it with `predict()`, which uses the unrounded parameters:

```{r}
# predict() wants a data frame: one row, one column per predictor
predict(line_fit, new_data = tibble(age = 45))$.pred
```

The two agree to within a few hundredths: the difference is only the
rounding.

```{r}
ggplot(train, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = b[1], slope = b[2],
              colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = 45, y = predict(line_fit, new_data = tibble(age = 45))$.pred,
           colour = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "Training patients, the fitted line, and the 45-year-old")
```

#### Task 1b — Predictions against measured glucose

The test patients were not used to fit the line. Predict their glucose and put
it next to what was measured.

```{r}
test_results <- test |>
  mutate(predicted = predict(line_fit, new_data = test)$.pred,
         gap = glucose - predicted)

test_results
```

```{r}
ggplot(test_results, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = b[1], slope = b[2],
              colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = age, y = glucose, yend = predicted),
               colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(y = glucose), colour = "darkorange", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "Test patients: measured (orange) and predicted (on the line)")
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. How far are the predictions from the measured glucose, typically?
> 2. All 16 predictions lie in a narrow band. Why?

#### Task 1c — Different training patients

Split again with a different seed, refit, and compare.

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
split_1 <- initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8)
train_1 <- training(split_1)

line_fit_1 <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = ______)

line_fit_1$fit$coefficients
predict(line_fit_1, new_data = tibble(age = ______))$.pred
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> Nothing about the model changes: `lm_model` is the same specification. Only the
> training patients change, and the patient you predict for is the same
> 45-year-old.

Twenty different splits, twenty different lines:

```{r}
lines_20 <- tibble()
for (s in 1:20) {
  set.seed(s)
  train_s <- training(initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8))
  fit_s <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = train_s)
  lines_20 <- bind_rows(lines_20, tibble(
    seed = s,
    intercept = fit_s$fit$coefficients[1],
    slope = fit_s$fit$coefficients[2]))
}

ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_abline(data = lines_20, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope),
              colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "The fitted line from 20 different training splits")
```

> **Think about it**
>
> Where do the 20 lines agree most, and where do they spread out? What does that
> mean for a prediction at age 25 compared with age 75?

### Part 2 — Add BMI

The same specification, `lm_model`, with a second predictor:

```{r}
plane_fit <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age + BMI, data = train)

plane_fit$fit$coefficients
```

$$\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \times \text{BMI}$$

With two predictors the model is no longer a line but a flat **plane** above
the age–BMI floor.

#### Task 2a — The same patient, now with a BMI of 30

```{r}
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_patient <- ______ + ______ * 45 + ______ * 30
predicted_patient
```

> **Stuck?**
>
> Three parameters, in the order printed: the intercept, the weight for age, the
> weight for BMI.

Check it with `predict()`:

```{r}
patient <- tibble(age = 45, BMI = 30)

predict(plane_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred
```

Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom. The red point is the patient,
sitting on the plane.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
# every combination of age and BMI on a fine grid
grid <- expand_grid(age = seq(20, 82, by = 0.5),
                    BMI = seq(19, 47, by = 0.5))
ages <- unique(grid$age)
bmis <- unique(grid$BMI)

# the plane's prediction at each grid point, as a matrix:
# one row per BMI value, one column per age
plane_matrix <- matrix(predict(plane_fit, new_data = grid)$.pred,
                       nrow = length(bmis))

fig_plane <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_markers(data = train, x = ~age, y = ~BMI, z = ~glucose,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                      name = "Training patients") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = plane_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.6, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("lightgrey", "grey")),
                      name = "Plane") |>
  plotly::add_markers(x = 45, y = 30,
                      z = predict(plane_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred,
                      marker = list(size = 7, color = "red"),
                      name = "Age 45, BMI 30") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Glucose (mg/dL)")))
fig_plane
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. In words, what does the BMI weight mean?
> 2. Adding BMI moved this patient's prediction by how much? Does a second
>    predictor guarantee better predictions?

### Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree

Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the
`fit()` and `predict()` calls stay the same.

```{r}
# 1. Specify: a regression tree, computed by rpart
tree_model <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_fit <- tree_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age + BMI, data = train)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, type = 3, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = "Blues", roundint = FALSE)
```

Each box asks a yes/no question. **Yes goes left, no goes right.** The number in
each leaf at the bottom is the prediction: the mean glucose of the training
patients who ended up there.

#### Task 3a — Follow the patient

Start at the top with the patient aged 45 with a BMI of 30. At each question,
go left or right. Which leaf do you reach, and what glucose does it predict?

Check it with `predict()`:

```{r}
predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred
```

Turn the plot. The orange surface is the tree, the grey one the plane from
Part 2.

```{r}
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
# the tree's prediction on the same grid as the plane
tree_matrix <- matrix(predict(tree_fit, new_data = grid)$.pred,
                      nrow = length(bmis))

fig_tree <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_markers(data = train, x = ~age, y = ~BMI, z = ~glucose,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                      name = "Training patients") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = tree_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.8, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("moccasin", "darkorange")),
                      name = "Tree") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = plane_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.5, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("lightgrey", "grey")),
                      name = "Plane") |>
  plotly::add_markers(x = 45, y = 30,
                      z = predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred,
                      marker = list(size = 7, color = "red"),
                      name = "Age 45, BMI 30 (tree)") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Glucose (mg/dL)")))
fig_tree
```

> **Think about it**
>
> 1. Describe the shape of the tree's surface. Why is it made of flat steps?
> 2. This tree never asks about BMI. What does that do to its surface, and why
>    might it have ignored BMI?
> 3. A new patient is 90 years old, older than anyone in the training data. What
>    do the plane and the tree predict, and why do they behave differently?

> **Learning points**
>
> - The steps are the same whatever the model: specify, fit on the training
>   patients, predict for new ones. Swapping linear regression for a tree
>   changed one line.
> - A linear model's prediction can be worked out by hand from its parameters; a
>   tree's prediction is read by following the questions to a leaf.
> - The fitted model depends on which patients were used for training.
> - A line or plane changes smoothly and keeps going beyond the data; a tree
>   predicts in flat steps and stays within the values it saw.
